issues.legal_issue: Revocation of a grant of probate operates prospectively and does not invalidate bona fide intermediate acts of an executor performed while the grant remains in force and in the course of administering the estate.
material_facts: The executor conveyed the property while the probate granted in his favour remained in force.
The probate was later revoked on the ground that two heirs had not been cited; the evidence did not establish that the revocation was based on fraud or forgery.
The conveyance was found to be bona fide and compatible with administration of the estate.
issues.conclusion: The later revocation did not invalidate the bona fide conveyance made during the subsistence of the probate.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 211, 227 and 263 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an executor derives authority from the will, and probate establishes the will from the testator’s death and validates intermediate acts. Revocation operates prospectively; it does not undo bona fide intermediate acts compatible with administration of the estate, although acts in breach of trust or incompatible with administration are not protected. Sections 221, 273, 297, 307 and 332 support this distinction. The Court relied on S. Parthasarathy Aiyar v. M. Subbaraya Gramany, Mt. Azimunnisa Begum v. Sirdar Ali Khan, Cherichi v. Ittianam, Sheonath Singh v. Madanlal, Hem Nolini Judah v. Isolyne Sarojbashini Bose, Komollochun Dutt v. Nilruttun Mundle, Mt. Ramanandi Kuer v. Mt. Kalawati Kuer, Akshay Kumar Pal v. Nandalal Das, and Valerine Basil Pais v. Gilbert William James Pais.

issues.legal_issue: A conveyance by an executor to a purchaser for value is binding on the estate and its heirs where the transaction is not proved fraudulent, the purchaser acts in good faith after reasonable care, and the heirs’ conduct allowed the executor to appear entitled to transfer the property.
material_facts: The will named the executor as a legatee of the property, and the property had been agreed to be sold while the testator was alive.
An advance under the sale agreement was paid directly to the testator, supporting the finding that he knew of and approved the proposed sale.
The executor obtained probate before the conveyance; the probate was later revoked for non-citation, while the prior application alleging fraud and forgery had been dismissed.
The purchaser searched the title documents, paid consideration, and incurred substantial costs in clearing encumbrances and developing the property.
The heirs did not establish fraud or collusion by the purchaser; the evidence showed that an heir knew of the will and that the heirs did not act to prevent the development over the ensuing years.
The purchaser later conveyed interests to further purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The conveyance to the developer was valid and binding on the heirs, the developer was a bona fide purchaser for value, and its subsequent alienations were valid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, is an exception to the rule that a person cannot convey a better title than they have. The transferee must establish that the transferor was the ostensible owner with the consent, express or implied, of the true owner, and that the transferee took reasonable care to ascertain the transferor’s authority and acted in good faith. The Court relied on Gurbaksh Singh v. Nikka Singh and Seshumull M. Shah v. Sayed Abdul Rashid. It also applied sections 211, 227 and 307 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and the principle in Valerine Basil Pais v. Gilbert William James Pais that a bona fide third party is not answerable for a propounder’s fraud or mistake. Under G.F.F. Foulkes v. A.S. Suppan Chettiar, a purchaser is not protected where the transaction gives notice that the executor is disposing of assets contrary to the will. Suspicious circumstances must be abnormal or not ordinarily expected, and the propounder must address circumstances raised by the objectors: Smt. Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose and Surendra Nath Chatterji v. Jahnavi Charan Mukherji. Fraud must be pleaded and proved; the Court found the lower courts’ inferences unsupported by the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent civil findings that rest on unsupported assumptions and inferences rather than evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court found fraud, collusion, and lack of bona fide purchase based on inferences from the speed and circumstances of the transaction.

The courts did not adequately consider material evidence, including the payment made directly to the testator, the grounds on which probate was revoked, and evidence concerning the heirs’ knowledge and conduct.
The findings of fraud or collusion against the purchaser lacked supporting pleadings and particulars.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court reviewed and set aside the concurrent findings because their inferential basis was unsupported and material circumstances had been overlooked.
issues.legal_principle: Although the Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent civil findings in special-leave appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, it may review an inferential process where the conclusions rest on assumptions or circumstances offering no direct or positive support, or where relevant evidence has been ignored. Inferences must reflect the realistic diversity of the facts rather than dead uniformity. The Court applied this principle in reviewing the lower courts’ findings.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal brought by special leave, concurrent findings based on unsupported inferences and reached without considering material evidence may be reviewed and set aside by the Supreme Court.

issues.legal_issue: A party is not barred from relying on a probate and will merely because it chose to proceed with an appeal without awaiting a separate decision on the will’s validity.
material_facts: Before the trial court, the defendants had sought a stay of the partition suit pending the probate proceedings, but the plaintiffs opposed the request and prevailed.
The plaintiffs themselves relied on alleged suspicious circumstances surrounding the will in the partition proceedings.
Before the High Court, the subsequent purchasers chose to proceed with the appeal rather than wait for the probate proceedings to conclude.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers were not precluded from relying on the probate and will to support the validity of the transaction and their claim to bona fide purchase.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the argument that the purchasers’ decision before the High Court amounted to a binding concession barring reliance on the probate or will. It considered the parties’ positions in the earlier proceedings, including the purchasers’ unsuccessful request for a stay and the plaintiffs’ reliance on the will’s alleged suspicious circumstances.
